title: Myths About the Brain
summary: Josh and Chuck work through a list of common myths about the brain. They cover whether the brain is gray (it has white matter, black substantia nigra from neuromelanin, and red coloring), the Mozart effect and the 1990s University of California, Irvine study that was taken out of context, the idea that a new wrinkle forms each time you learn something, whale and dolphin brain size versus body size ratio, subliminal advertising and James Vicary's 1957 popcorn and Coca-Cola claims, whether brain damage is permanent and brain plasticity (including a woman with one brain hemisphere who has binocular vision), the ten percent myth and its possible origin with William James, savantism and the frontal lobe "tyranny" theory, whether drugs and alcohol create holes or kill brain cells (thiamine deficiency and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome), and a listener mail about fecal transplants and a childhood memory of a father's bathroom habits.

segments.title: Opening and brain myths preview
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on ten myths about the brain, noting they will cover only some of the list and that a couple were covered before.

segments.title: Is the brain gray?
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the idea that the brain is gray, noting gray matter and white matter, the black substantia nigra linked to motor control and Parkinson's, and neuromelanin, a pigment thought to remove heavy metals.

segments.title: Mozart effect
segments.summary: The Mozart effect is described, starting with a 1950s ear, nose and throat doctor's claims and a 1990s University of California, Irvine study. The hosts say the study was taken out of context and results could not be replicated, though learning music has other benefits.

segments.title: Brain wrinkles and folding
segments.summary: The hosts say the myth that a new wrinkle forms each time you learn something is false. They note the brain's folds, or gyri and sulci, are present by about forty weeks and are folded because the brain is larger than the skull.

segments.title: Brain size: humans vs whales and other animals
segments.summary: The myth that humans have the biggest brain is addressed. Sperm whale brains weigh about seventeen pounds, but the brain-to-body ratio matters more; humans are about one to fifty, most mammals one to one eighty, and birds about one to two hundred twenty. The cerebral cortex is discussed as what sets humans apart.

segments.title: Subliminal messages and popcorn
segments.summary: The hosts cover subliminal advertising, including James Vicary's 1957 claim of sales increases for popcorn and drinks, the FCC ban, Vicary later admitting he lied about results, and a Canadian test. They speculate about how the messages were worded.

segments.title: Brain damage, plasticity and the one-hemisphere girl
segments.summary: The myth that brain damage is always permanent is refuted. Neurons damaged cannot regrow, but brain plasticity forms new connections, as with stroke patients relearning speech. A girl with one brain hemisphere has binocular vision because her optic nerve rerouted to the other side.

segments.title: The ten percent myth and savantism
segments.summary: The hosts say the ten percent myth is false, with a possible origin in a William James quote from the early 1900s. They discuss the frontal lobe theory of savantism, in which disruption of frontal lobe control may free other abilities.

segments.title: Drugs, alcohol and brain cell death
segments.summary: The hosts say drugs do not create holes in the brain, and that some long-term drug use may make parts of the brain grow. Alcohol damages dendrites rather than killing brain cells; Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome stems from thiamine deficiency common in alcoholics.

segments.title: Listener mail on fecal transplants
segments.summary: Listener Jacob Carnes writes about having norovirus after the fecal transplant episode, suggesting kombucha for gut flora, and recounts his childhood memory of his father smoking in the bathroom.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask for habit-breaking tips and give contact information for Twitter, Facebook, email and the website.
